e.t: This word describes someone who is “innocent”—not guilty of the wrongdoing under discussion. It functions as a description of a person’s moral or legal standing, rather than naming an action. In the Greek New Testament, it appears twice, both times in Matthew 27, and both occurrences are rendered “innocent.” The word therefore presents innocence as a recognizable condition attributed to a person. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and argument.

e.t: This word means “to report” or “to tell”—to make information known to others. It describes communicating something that has been learned, witnessed, or received, rather than merely keeping it private. In the Greek New Testament, it appears 14 times, showing a recurring use for announcing or sharing information. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on what is being communicated and to whom, but its central idea remains the clear transmission of information.

Ananias is a personal name, identifying people rather than describing a quality, action, or object. In the Greek New Testament, it is rendered as “Ananias” and occurs 11 times in 10 verses, all in Acts. The name appears in passages involving individuals known by this name, including references in Acts 5 and Acts 9. Its meaning as used here is therefore primarily identification: it tells the reader who a person is, while the surrounding passage is needed to distinguish which Ananias is being mentioned.

This word describes someone who is not resentful—one who does not keep bitterness or hostility toward others. It points to an attitude free from stored grievance rather than merely a temporary absence of anger. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, so its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage. Its central meaning remains clear: not resentful.

e.t: This word means “disbelieve”: to refuse to accept something as true or trustworthy. It describes a response of unbelief toward a report, testimony, or claim. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs eight times, showing that it is used in several passages to describe people who do not accept what they have heard or been told. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context, but its central idea remains rejecting belief rather than receiving something as true.

This word means “using up.” It describes the action of using something until its available use is exhausted. It functions as a verb, focusing on what happens to something through use rather than naming a person, object, or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Colossians 2:22. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is the completion or exhaustion of something through being used.

Archelaus is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or general object. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, in Matthew 2:22, and is rendered as “Archelaus.” Because it is a proper name, its basic meaning is the person it identifies; the surrounding passage is needed to explain that person’s role in the verse. The name itself does not function as a common noun or verb.

me: ADVerb or adverb and particle combined

e.t: This word means “carefully” or “securely,” describing how an action is carried out. As an adverb, it adds the sense that something is done with attention, caution, or dependable security rather than carelessly. It appears three times in the Greek New Testament, in Mark and Acts. Its precise emphasis in any particular verse depends on the action and surrounding words, but its central idea remains careful or secure performance.

This word means “until” and marks the point up to which an action, condition, or period continues. It sets a time boundary: something remains true or keeps happening before that stated point, and the wording directs attention to what happens when the limit is reached. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 49 times, showing regular use for expressing temporal limits. Its basic sense remains the same whether the boundary concerns an event, a period, or another stated time.

This word means “dispersion” or “scattering”—the condition of being spread away from a central place or group. It is a noun describing a dispersed people or community rather than the act of scattering itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, appearing in John, James, and 1 Peter. Its precise reference in each passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to kill,” describing the act of causing someone’s death. It is a verb, so it expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The word occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, both times in Acts. Its basic meaning remains direct and concrete: someone is put to death. The surrounding passage determines who performs the action and why, but the word itself identifies the deadly act without adding a separate motive or spiritual interpretation.

“Image” is the central meaning of this Greek New Testament word. It identifies something presented as an image, whether the word is used in a statement, comparison, or description. The word occurs 23 times in the Greek New Testament, across 20 verses, so its basic sense appears in a range of passages rather than only one setting. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding words and passage.

e.t: This word means “to go into great detail about” or “to investigate.” It describes careful, intensive attention to a matter rather than a brief or general consideration. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Colossians 2:18. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the word’s precise force in that passage must be understood from its context. Its basic sense points to examining or discussing something closely and extensively. [Evidence: p03:word:greek-nt:G1687:identity; p03:word:greek-nt:G1687:occurrences]

e.t: This word describes something happening at night, especially while it is still dark before daylight. It functions as a time expression, telling when an action occurs rather than naming a person, place, or object. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, at Mark 1:35. Its basic sense is therefore a nighttime setting; the surrounding verse determines the particular action being described. The two stated meanings emphasize both the nighttime period and the darkness that remains.

e.t: This Greek New Testament verb means “to awake” or “to wake up.” It describes the action of becoming awake, whether from ordinary sleep or in a figurative setting where waking is expressed. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, at John 11:11. Its basic meaning is therefore focused and clear: someone is awakened or becomes awake. The surrounding verse and passage determine how that action functions in its particular setting.

This word means “to silence”—to stop someone from speaking or prevent speech from continuing. It describes an action directed toward a speaker, rather than merely becoming quiet oneself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Titus 1:11, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its central idea remains clear: bringing speech to an end or rendering a person unable to continue speaking.

This word means “a word” or “word.” It refers to a verbal expression—a unit of speech used to communicate something. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs only once, in Hebrews 7:9. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the word’s precise force in that sentence must be understood from its context. Its basic sense remains a spoken or written word rather than an action, person, or place.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to come” or “to reach.” It describes arriving at a place, person, or intended point. In its two New Testament occurrences, it is rendered “reach,” including the idea of reaching people or territory within the proper scope of one’s work. The word functions as an action: someone comes to or reaches what lies ahead. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense remains movement toward an intended destination or boundary.

“Than” is a comparison word. It connects two people, things, or choices and indicates that one is being preferred, valued, or regarded above the other. Its meaning is relational: it does not describe an object by itself, but helps express a comparison between alternatives. This Greek New Testament word occurs once, in John 12:43. Its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic function remains to mark comparison.

This word means “heat,” referring to warmth or high temperature. It appears once in the Greek New Testament, in Acts 28:3. Its basic sense identifies the warmth produced by fire or another source, rather than describing a person, action, or spiritual quality. The surrounding verse determines how this reference to heat functions in that specific passage, but the word itself carries the straightforward idea of heat.

Jason is a personal name used to identify a man in the Greek New Testament. It is not a description of a character trait, action, or spiritual condition, but a proper name. The name occurs five times, appearing four times in Acts and once in Romans. Because the available wording consistently renders it as “Jason,” its meaning is simply the person’s name rather than a translatable title or ordinary descriptive term.

This Greek New Testament word means “strength,” referring to the ability or capacity to act, endure, or accomplish something with force. It can describe human strength offered in devotion to God and the mighty strength associated with God’s work. The word occurs ten times in the Greek New Testament, and its central sense remains strength throughout those uses. Its precise emphasis in a particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

The word means “beginning” or “creation.” It can refer to the starting point of something, or to creation as what came into existence. These meanings are closely related: creation marks the beginning of the created order, while a beginning marks the point from which something starts. In the Greek New Testament, the word occurs 11 times. Its precise sense in a particular verse depends on how the surrounding sentence uses the idea of beginning or creation.

This word means “preparation,” referring to making something ready for its intended purpose. It describes readiness or the act of being equipped, rather than the final result itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Ephesians 4:12, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its central idea remains the movement from being unready to being prepared for useful work or service.

“Dissipation” describes a condition in which a person or resource is spent away through careless excess. It points to wastefulness and a lack of restraint rather than steady, purposeful living. This Greek New Testament word occurs once, in Luke 21:34. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is dissipation—being weakened, scattered, or consumed instead of carefully guarded.

This word refers to “administration”—the organized direction or management of a responsibility. It names a function rather than an action performed once, so it can describe the orderly handling of matters entrusted to someone. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Corinthians 12:28. Without the verse text, its exact emphasis there should be understood from the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains responsible administration.

e.t: This word means “to stone” or “to throw stones”—to attack someone by hurling stones at them. It describes a deliberate physical action, not merely the presence of stones. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs seven times across seven verses, including accounts involving Jesus’ enemies and the killing of Stephen. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains the act of throwing stones at a person.【p03:word:greek-nt:G3036:identity】【p03:word:greek-nt:G3036:occurrences】

This word means a tomb or burial place—the place where a dead person is laid. It can refer to one tomb or to multiple tombs, depending on the sentence. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs eight times, including references to tombs associated with the dead and to the tomb where Jesus was laid. The word itself identifies a burial place; the surrounding passage determines the particular tomb being discussed.

Nympha is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than describing an object, action, or quality. In the Greek New Testament, this name occurs once, in Colossians 4:15. The name itself does not establish the person’s character, role, beliefs, or circumstances; those details require the surrounding verse and passage. Its meaning at the lexical level is simply the person’s name, Nympha.

This word means “so.” It is used to connect what has been said with a resulting conclusion, much like saying “therefore” or “then” in ordinary English. Its role is brief but important: it signals that the next statement follows logically from the preceding words. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, at John 18:37. The exact force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding conversation, but its basic meaning remains a connective “so.”

Parmenas is a personal name, identifying someone called Parmenas. It is not presented here as a common word describing an action, quality, or object, so its meaning is the person’s name rather than a broader concept. In the Greek New Testament, Parmenas occurs once, in Acts 6:5. The available rendering preserves the name as “Parmenas,” without offering another lexical meaning. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and verse text.

e.h: A Proverb or Figure of Speech
e.t: This word refers to a proverb or figure of speech—a saying expressed in a memorable or indirect way rather than as a plain statement. It identifies a kind of saying used to communicate meaning through a familiar comparison or patterned expression. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs five times in four verses, chiefly in John and once in 2 Peter. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding words and passage.

e.t: “To carry” means to bear or transport something, and it can also describe carrying something around. It is a Greek New Testament verb describing the action of moving or bearing something. This word occurs three times in the Greek New Testament, so its central meaning remains consistent while its precise force depends on the sentence where it appears. The English rendering “carry” reflects its basic sense.

This word means “many” or “most,” describing a larger number or the greater part of a group. It is used when attention is given to quantity, especially when something involves more people or items than others. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times, each in a different verse. Its precise force—whether “many” or “most”—depends on the sentence and surrounding context.

e.t: This word describes something done beforehand—an action completed or undertaken in advance. It can express “having done beforehand,” “to commit beforehand,” or “to do beforehand,” depending on how it functions in the sentence. Its central idea is priority in time: the action occurs before another event or point being discussed. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, at Romans 3:25. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain its precise force there, but its basic meaning remains an action performed or committed in advance.

This Greek New Testament word means “trumpet” and names the instrument itself. It is a noun used for a trumpet or trumpets, including references in Matthew, 1 Corinthians, 1 Thessalonians, Hebrews, and Revelation. The word occurs 11 times in the Greek New Testament, with six occurrences in Revelation. Its exact significance in any particular passage comes from the surrounding verse and context, but its basic meaning remains the trumpet as an instrument that can be sounded.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to bury” or “to entomb,” describing the act of placing a dead person in a grave or tomb. It is an action word concerned with burial itself, rather than with mourning, the grave’s location, or a person’s identity. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Acts 8:2. Its exact force in that verse is understood through the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the act of burying or entombing someone.

e.t: This word means “be with” or “to be with,” describing someone’s presence alongside another person or group. It expresses being together rather than acting alone. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, showing this is a specific verb for shared presence, not a broad description of every kind of relationship. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but the central idea remains simple: one person is present with another. The word appears once in Luke and once in Acts.

gl: to partake in a feast together

e.t: This word means “to feast with” or “to partake in a feast together.” It describes people sharing a meal or feast in company with others, emphasizing participation in the same gathering rather than merely eating alone. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, once in 2 Peter and once in Jude. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains shared participation in a feast. The word therefore points to joining others at a common meal or celebration, whether the setting is viewed positively or critically.

me: ADVerb or adverb and particle combined

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “completely” or “perfectly.” It describes something done or understood in a full, complete way, expressing the highest degree rather than something partial or unfinished. As an adverb, it explains how fully an action or condition is present. It occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in 1 Peter 1:13; its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This word means “arrogance” or “pride”—an attitude of thinking too highly of oneself and elevating oneself above others. It describes a self-exalting inward posture rather than ordinary confidence. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Mark 7:22. Its listed English rendering is “pride,” which closely expresses the central idea. The precise force of the word in that occurrence depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This word means “lukewarm,” describing something that is only mildly warm rather than hot. It is an adjective used to characterize a condition or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Revelation 3:16. Its basic meaning is straightforward: it identifies something lacking full heat, intensity, or warmth. The precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself refers to a tepid or lukewarm state.

e.t: This word means “to slander” or “to be slandered”: it concerns speaking falsely or harmfully against someone, or being treated that way. As a verb, it can describe either the act of attacking another person’s reputation or the experience of receiving such accusations. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Corinthians 4:13, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage.
